dataset.name: Throughfall-Reduction Drying Effects on Soil Moisture and Soil Temperature at 30-Minute Intervals Four Lowland Panamanian Forests
description: Climatic drying is predicted for many tropical forests, yet effects on soil properties across moisture and soil gradients within tropical forests remain poorly characterized, hampering predictions of forest-climate feedbacks. We hypothesized that drying would suppress soil CO2 fluxes (i.e., respiration) in already-drier tropical forests by further reductions in soil moisture, but increases CO2 fluxes in wetter tropical forests by alleviating anaerobiosis and soil saturation. We measured soil CO2 fluxes, soil moisture, soil temperature, and forest floor biomass during wet-dry cycles (2015 – 2022) in four Panamanian forests that vary in rainfall and soil fertility. We also surveyed all tree species and identified to species in 2018 and 2019.

We found that soil moisture peaked in the wet season and declined in the dry season. Measured soil CO2 fluxes declined in the dry season and peaked in the early wet season ahead of peak soil moisture, resulting in a lower soil moisture optimum for respiration than previously modeled. Chronic throughfall exclusion also suppressed soil moisture across the four forests, and also initially suppressed soil CO2 fluxes across forests. There was sustained suppression of soil CO2 fluxes after four years in the wettest forest only (-28 ± 4% during the dry season), but elevated soil CO2 fluxes in a fertile forest after four years (+75 ± 28% during the late wet season). The unexpected negative drying effect in the wettest, most infertile forest could have resulted from reduced vertical flushing of nutrients into soils, as the drying effect increased with time. Including hydro-nutrient interactions in ecosystem models could improve predictions of tropical forest-climate feedbacks (Cusack et al. 2023).

Datasets here include .csv and .xls files for volumetric soil moisture (volume/volume) and soil temperature (°C). Data were taken at 30-minute intervals at 5cm and 20cm depths using permanent probes and data loggers (see methods). Data presented are from 2018-2019. There is also a .kml file that includes coordinates for all 32 plots included in the study of four forests (n = 4 throughfall reduction and n = 4 control plots per site). No special software is needed to open these files.

measurementTechnique:
Study Sites & Design:
This study was conducted in four distinct lowland seasonal tropical forests located across gradients in rainfall and soil fertility on the Isthmus of Panama. The sites are a subset of a larger network of ~50 1-ha long-term plots maintained by the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI) in the Panamanian lowlands. The four forests span an increase of 1,000 mm MAP, and include three forests on strongly weathered, low fertility soils at low (site GIG), mid (site P12), and high rainfall (site SC), and one forest on high-fertility soils paired with the infertile forest at mid-rainfall (site P13). This design was used to help disentangle effects of mean annual precipitation (MAP) and soil fertility on soil responses to seasonal and experimental drying. The four forests included here were: a forest at 2350 mm MAP on strongly weathered, infertile soil on the Gigante Peninsula (GIG), two paired forests at 2500 mm MAP on the Buena Vista Peninsula, one with strongly weathered infertile soil (Plot 12 [P12]), and one with less weathered fertile soil (Plot 13 [P13]), and a forest at 3300 mm MAP on strongly weathered infertile soil on the Caribbean coast in the San Lorenzo forest at Sherman Crane (SC).
In each forest, we began monitoring soils in 2015 along 4 50-m transects per site, and then established four pairs of permanent 10 x 10 m plots nearby in 2017. One plot in each pair was assigned to the partial throughfall exclusion experiment. Plots were paired based on proximity and topography. We situated plots on relatively flat ground at least 10 m apart from each other, and in locations where large trees (DBH> 30 – 40 cm) were absent to avoid having a plot dominated by the root system of a single plant. The control plot in each pair was used to add to the long-term date set of soil CO2 flux and other properties initiated in 2015.
In the manipulation plot in each pair, we constructed partial throughfall exclusion structure that extended 12 m x 12 m over the plot, such that the structure extending 1 m beyond the plot edge in every direction to avoid edge effects. We trenched partial throughfall exclusion plots to 50 cm depth, lined the vertical sides of the trenches with heavy duty plastic, and then backfilled the trenches to inhibit plants in exclusion plots from foraging for water outside of the plots. The experiment was designed to mimic a chronic drying scenario, diverting throughfall from above each plot. We named the partial throughfall exclusion experiment PAnama Rainforest CHanges with Experimental Drying (PARCHED).
Structure construction is summarized here, with further details in (Dietterich et al. 2022). Construction started in 2017. Aluminum tubes with nominal diameter 32 mm were hammered vertically into the ground in a grid pattern. These aluminum tubes supported horizontal PVC tubes of the same diameter at heights peaking in the center line of the plot. Transparent polycarbonate laminates were cut into strips of approximately 33 cm x 2 m and attached to the PVC tubes using nuts, bolts, and washers, such that they initially covered ~50% of the plot area and sloped from ~2.3 m height at the midline of the plot to ~1.1 m height at the outer edge of the structure, forming a ~11.3º angle. We monitored topography and surface water flow to ensure that water running off the laminates did not run back into the exclusion plots, and in the few cases where we observed evidence of this, we used additional strips of laminas and segments of PVC tubing to construct ground-level barriers to water flow. We completed plot construction in 2018 on May 16 (P13), June 12 (P12), July 26 (SC), and December 3 (GIG). In August of 2021, we added additional roofing to each structure to bring the area covered to ~70% to increase the intensity of the drying treatment.
Every three weeks, at the time of soil monitoring, leaf litter was brushed off roofing and into the plots, using broom heads mounted on telescoping poles to sweep leaf litter back into its plot in a distributed way. Roofing laminates were also scrubbed with rough sponges periodically to keep them clear and free from excessive moss and mold. We repaired damages to plots from fallen trees, branches, and large fruits as soon as possible after detection every month.

Data Collection for this data set:
Data for volumetric soil moisture and soil temperature from soil probes are given on 30-minute intervals at 5cm and 20cm depths in the four forests in each plot per treatment (n = 4 throughfall reduction, 4 control per site). This data for 30-minute variation in soil moisture and temperature was collected using permanent 10HS soil moisture and RT-1 temperature probes from METER Group installed at 5 cm depth and 20 cm depth in a central location in each plot. These were connected to an EM50 or ZL6 data logger in each plot, recording data from May 2018 to Oct. 2022. Data were downloaded on a monthly basis and compiled. Data were cleaned, removing clear outliers (>99 percentile) but conservatively retaining data if no clear equipment malfunction. These data were used to confirm seasonal soil moisture and temperature trends as indicated from the less frequent measurements that were concurrent with CO2 fluxes measures (see other related data sets).The frequent 30-minute volumetric soil probe data show seasonal patterns in moisture and temperature for the four forests, with steep declines in soil moisture during the dry season, and then gradual increases in soil moisture over the course of the wet season, as described further in the associated citation.
